title: Favorite Resources
text:
Because sometimes a magpie-brain needs a shiny little treat.
RDM Weekly, from Crystal Lewis (Free)
Substack-hosted free newsletter, weekly roundup of resources for Research Data Management. Cute memes, too. Author of Data Management in Large-Scale Education Research, a must-have for folks in my field. I had the good fortune to meet Crystal at a conference in 2018 and she is an absolute gem.
R-Bloggers (Free)
Near-daily news and tutorials contributed by hundreds of individual bloggers and aggregated in one place. I’m convinced no one actually reads every post, but a quick skim of the titles will often bring me a gem I wouldn’t have come across otherwise. Note that their ‘R Jobs’ is wildly, comically out of date.
Census Updates, from U.S. Census Bureau (Free)
Occasional email updates and press releases regarding Census data products, workshops, and resources. I’ve taken part in a few great webinars thanks to these communications, as they’re not widely advertised otherwise.
JournalClub ($)
Daily newsletter with embedded video, each summarizing a recent journal article related to machine learning, modeling, software development, and MANY adjacent topics. I don’t get to all of them, but I do really like seeing how people in other fields are solving their emerging problems even if I have to draw heavily on context clues for the specialized vocabulary. They also very deliberately are not using AI tools to create these summaries. And the writing itself is SO efficient and straightforward.

Gosh am I grateful for the R-Ladies+ community! Thanks to the Santa Barbara crew of this incredible global network, I came across a terrific tutorial from Sam Shanny-Csik: “Creating your personal website using Quarto” published at URL.
I’ve been in the weeds with Quarto for a couple years now, most recently iterating resumes and cover letters during my job search. And of course Jorge and I used Quarto extensively during our time together with HISD (teamwork!). Do I need to do a bit more work in updating fonts and colors? Probably. Do I need to remove the lingering placeholder text on the Resources page? Of course.

title: About Me
text:
Data & Policy Analytics Leader | K-12 Education Strategy | Causal Inference, Forecasting & Enrollment Modeling | Grants & Financial Stewardship | Data Governance | Program Evaluation | Research Partnerships
Data and policy leader with 10+ years of experience using analytics, causal inference, and strategic planning to support decision-making in large K-12 school systems.
My work sits at the intersection of education policy, finance, data science, and operational strategy. I translate complex administrative data into insights that help districts allocate resources, expand program access, strengthen compliance, and improve student outcomes.
At Houston ISD, I have led analytics initiatives supporting enrollment strategy, pre-K expansion, staffing models, capital planning, grant implementation, and research partnerships. My work has helped district leaders make decisions affecting hundreds of schools, millions of student records, and major public investments.
Selected impact includes: • Led enrollment and retention modeling that preserved $65.7M in state funding by identifying strategies to retain 4,570 students. • Directed analytics informing pre-K expansion across 160+ campuses, increasing classroom capacity and improving access for families. • Supported a RAND randomized controlled trial of Zearn Math across 32,000+ students and 845 teachers. • Managed $62.3M in federal grant programs with compliant reporting and zero audit findings. • Built reproducible analytics pipelines and decision dashboards used by district leadership for staffing, program evaluation, and capital planning.
My background combines advanced statistical analysis, program evaluation, financial management, and policy implementation. I regularly work with large administrative datasets covering millions of student records and apply methods such as clustering, simulation modeling, causal inference, and forecasting.
I have also authored multiple program evaluations and research publications focused on STEM education, student outcomes, and teacher incentives, and have collaborated with universities and national research organizations.
I am motivated by a simple goal: use rigorous data analysis and thoughtful questions to help education systems make better strategic decisions that expand opportunity and improve outcomes for students.

title: Working with US Census Data
text:
More than Once A Decade

In 1790, first national count — just six questions!
In 1902, Congress established the Census Bureau as a permanent agency
In 2026, in the Department of Commerce
Today, the Census Bureau conducts more than 130 different surveys.
- Decennial Census of Population and Housing. Every ten years, required by constitution.
- American Community Survey. Annual survey on the social and economic needs of communities.
- Economic Census. Five-year measure of American business and the economy at the national, state, and local levels.
- Current Population Survey. Monthly survey of households on how Americans work — the types of jobs held, the hours worked, and salary information.


In 1902, Congress established the Census Bureau as a permanent agency that would collect vital information and develop statistics representing the American people, including where and how they live.
Distribute more than $675 billion in federal funds to local, state, and tribal governments each year.
Plus, States and communities use census data to allocate funding for neighborhood improvements, public health, education, transportation, and more.
Sources: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sis/about/students101.html

title: Working with US Census Data
text:
Geographies: Big to Small
< image >



Standard hierarchy of US Census geographic entities


Tract: Census tracts ideally contain about 4,000 people and 1,600 housing units.
Block Group: A statistical subdivision of a census tract, generally defined to contain between 600 and 3,000 people and 240 and 1,200 housing units. The smallest geographic unit for which the Census Bureau tabulates sample data. A sub-division of a census tract.
Block: A block is the smallest geographic unit for which the Census Bureau tabulates decennial census data. Many blocks correspond to individual city blocks bounded by streets, but blocks – especially in rural areas – may include many square miles and may have some boundaries that are not streets.

  mutate(housing_status =

      variable == "H3_002N" ~ "Occupied", 
      variable == "H3_003N" ~ "Vacant"
    )) |> 
  select(-variable)

ggplot(gulf_counties2,

text:
Redistricting Dataset (PL)
Smaller dataset produced from DHC for redistricting under Public Law 94-171 (PL)
The summary file tables include:
P1. – Race
P2. – Hispanic or Latino, and not Hispanic or Latino by Race
P3. – Race for the Population 18 Years and Over
P4. – Hispanic or Latino, by Race for the Population 18 Years and Over
P5. – Group Quarters Population by Major Group Quarters Type
H1. – Occupancy Status (Housing)
